info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 11.1: Aligning Translation Sentences and Authoring Interlinear Glosses by Hand.

name.text: 01 Question: The Purpose of Alignment in Digital Critical Editions

questiontext.text: How does digital translation alignment transform the relationship between source texts and translations compared to traditional print layouts?

generalfeedback.text: Digital translation alignment transforms a translation from a passive facing-page paraphrase into an explicit, verifiable computational claim about textual meaning.

answer.text: It establishes an explicit bipartite graph of machine-readable correspondences, turning the translation into an accountable, verifiable analytic commentary.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital alignment treats parallel texts as formal bipartite graphs, exposing the exact mechanics of translational interpretation to computational scrutiny.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for translations by automatically translating ancient texts into modern vernaculars on the fly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment links historical human translations to their sources rather than replacing them with real-time automated translations.

answer.text: It replaces all linguistic apparatuses with simple side-by-side print facsimiles.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Facing-page print layouts leave correspondences implicit; digital alignment makes them formal and machine-readable.

answer.text: It converts source texts into monolingual token streams to discard target-language variation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital alignment preserves and models bilingual correspondences rather than flattening texts into monolingual streams.

name.text: 02 Question: Monolingual Editions vs. Parallel Bitexts

questiontext.text: What defines a parallel bitext in computational philology and translation studies?

generalfeedback.text: A bitext is a compound data structure linking two languages as an explicit bipartite graph, exposing cross-lingual divergence that facing-page layouts conceal.

answer.text: A single compound data structure linking two language versions via a formal bipartite graph of translational correspondences.

feedback.text: Correct. A bitext is not merely two texts placed side by side, but a unified compound data structure encoding explicit cross-lingual links.

answer.text: A monolingual edition that includes two separate apparatus criticus layers for scribal variants.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes a complex monolingual apparatus, not a parallel bitext linking two different languages.

answer.text: Two unaligned plain-text files stored in the same repository directory without structural cross-references.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unlinked texts lack the bipartite relational graph that defines a true bitext.

answer.text: A bilingual dictionary that lists isolated lemma translations without sentence context.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A bitext consists of connected parallel text streams rather than isolated dictionary entries.

name.text: 03 Question: The 4-Line Interlinear Glossed Text (IGT) Architecture

questiontext.text: In the standard four-line Interlinear Glossed Text (IGT) architecture, what is the specific function of Line 2?

generalfeedback.text: Four-line IGT separates surface orthography, morphemic segmentation, grammatical glossing, and idiomatic translation into four synchronized, machine-readable tiers.

answer.text: It presents the source text segmented into constituent morphemes (prefixes, roots, affixes, clitics) separated by standardized boundary symbols.

feedback.text: Correct. Line 2 isolates morphological components with hyphens and clitic markers, enabling exact 1-to-1 alignment with Line 3 glosses.

answer.text: It provides an idiomatic, fluent translation of the complete sentence enclosed in quotation marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The free idiomatic translation belongs on Line 4, not Line 2.

answer.text: It preserves the unsegmented historical surface orthography exactly as transcribed from the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The unsegmented historical surface text belongs on Line 1.

answer.text: It lists uppercase grammatical category abbreviations and lowercase lexical meanings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The grammatical and lexical gloss tier belongs on Line 3.

name.text: 04 Question: Leipzig Glossing Rules: Rule 1 (Word-by-Word Alignment)

questiontext.text: What does Leipzig Glossing Rule 1 strictly require regarding whitespace in interlinear glosses?

generalfeedback.text: Leipzig Rule 1 requires exact whitespace token synchronization so that every source word aligns with exactly one gloss token.

answer.text: Glosses must be left-aligned with corresponding source words, and whitespace is reserved exclusively as a delimiter between distinct word units.

feedback.text: Correct. Rule 1 dictates exact whitespace token synchronization so that each source word corresponds to exactly one gloss token.

answer.text: Whitespace may be freely inserted inside multi-word glosses to improve visual formatting on web pages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inserting unescaped whitespace inside a gloss breaks the word token count and causes downstream alignment collapse.

answer.text: Every letter in a gloss must be separated from adjacent letters by a single space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spaces separate words, not individual characters within a morpheme or gloss.

answer.text: Source words and glosses must be separated by commas rather than spaces or tabs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leipzig Rule 1 relies on standard whitespace tokenization, not comma-separated values.

name.text: 05 Question: Leipzig Glossing Rules: Rule 2 (Morpheme-by-Morpheme Correspondence)

questiontext.text: How does Leipzig Glossing Rule 2 govern the relationship between hyphens in Line 2 and Line 3?

generalfeedback.text: Leipzig Rule 2 mandates that every hyphen in the segmented source text must pair with an identical hyphen in the gloss tier.

answer.text: Every hyphen indicating a concatenative morpheme boundary in the segmented source text must pair with an identical hyphen in the gloss tier.

feedback.text: Correct. Rule 2 mandates exact morpheme-by-morpheme parity; unbalanced hyphens invalidate the alignment structure.

answer.text: Hyphens are used only in the English translation on Line 4 to link compound words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hyphens mark concatenative morpheme boundaries on Line 2 and Line 3.

answer.text: Line 2 must contain twice as many hyphens as Line 3 to account for inflectional prefixes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The number and sequential order of hyphens must be strictly identical between Line 2 and Line 3.

answer.text: Hyphens are optional and may be omitted whenever a root contains more than two syllables.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hyphens are mandatory structural delimiters for all concatenative morpheme boundaries.

name.text: 06 Question: Leipzig Glossing Rules: Rule 3 (Grammatical Category Labels and Small Caps)

questiontext.text: Under Leipzig Glossing Rule 3, how are lexical translations differentiated from grammatical categories in the gloss tier?

generalfeedback.text: Leipzig Rule 3 requires lexical translations in lowercase and grammatical categories in standard uppercase abbreviations, preserving clear boundaries between meaning and morphology.

answer.text: Lexical roots are rendered in lowercase letters, while grammatical categories and inflectional morphemes are rendered in standard uppercase abbreviations.

feedback.text: Correct. Rule 3 enforces lowercase for semantic translations and uppercase abbreviations for grammatical features (e.g. NOM, PST, 3SG).

answer.text: Lexical roots are written in uppercase, while grammatical categories are written in lowercase.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That inverts Rule 3, causing text-mining algorithms to confuse grammatical tags with English lexical words.

answer.text: Lexical roots must be enclosed in parentheses, while grammatical categories are enclosed in quotation marks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rule 3 relies on capitalization conventions (small caps / uppercase vs. lowercase), not quotes or parentheses.

answer.text: Grammatical categories are represented by numerical codes from 1 to 100 rather than alphabetic abbreviations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard Leipzig abbreviations use mnemonic alphabetic strings like NOM, ACC, AOR, and IND.

name.text: 07 Question: Leipzig Glossing Rules: Rule 4 (Multi-Word and Complex Glosses)

questiontext.text: According to Leipzig Glossing Rule 4, what punctuation symbols must be used for fused grammatical features and multi-word translations respectively?

generalfeedback.text: Use periods (.) for fused grammatical features and underscores (_) for multi-word translations to preserve exact token counts without whitespace errors.

answer.text: Periods (.) join fused grammatical features within a single morpheme, while underscores (_) or periods join multi-word lexical translations.

feedback.text: Correct. Periods mark portmanteau/fused grammatical categories (e.g., ACC.M.SG), while underscores prevent whitespace in multi-word glosses (e.g., turn_mind_to).

answer.text: Hyphens (-) are used for fused features, and spaces are used for multi-word translations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hyphens are reserved for segmentable concatenative morpheme boundaries (Rule 2), and spaces break token alignment (Rule 1).

answer.text: Semicolons (;) join fused features, and forward slashes (/) join multi-word translations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Semicolons and slashes are non-standard in Leipzig Rule 4.

answer.text: Angle brackets (< >) join fused features, and equals signs (=) join multi-word translations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Angle brackets denote infixes (Rule 7) and equals signs denote clitics (Rule 6).

name.text: 08 Question: Leipzig Glossing Rules: Rule 5 (Person and Number Combinations)

questiontext.text: How does Leipzig Glossing Rule 5 format person and number combinations, and how are subject-object pronominal interactions represented?

generalfeedback.text: Leipzig Rule 5 unifies person and number into unpunctuated tokens (1SG, 3PL) and uses relational markers (>) for subject-object pronominal affixes.

answer.text: Person and number are conjoined without punctuation (e.g., 1SG, 3PL), and subject-object pronominal markers are joined by a right arrow (>) or colon.

feedback.text: Correct. Person and number form unified agreement blocks (1SG, 2PL), while subject acting upon object is marked with > (e.g., 3SG.M>1SG).

answer.text: Person and number must be separated by a hyphen (e.g., 1-SG, 3-PL).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inserting hyphens falsely implies that person and number are separable concatenative morphemes.

answer.text: Person is written as a Roman numeral and number is written as a spelled-out word (e.g., I.SINGULAR).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leipzig Rule 5 uses standard alphanumeric abbreviations like 1SG, 2PL, 3DU.

answer.text: Subject-object interactions must be split into two separate words separated by whitespace.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Splitting across whitespace violates Rule 1 word-token synchronization.

name.text: 09 Question: Advanced Leipzig Operators: Clitics, Reduplication, and Infixes

questiontext.text: Which punctuation operators correspond correctly to clitics, infixes, and reduplication in the Leipzig Glossing Rules?

generalfeedback.text: Use equals signs (=) for clitics, angle brackets (< >) for infixes, and tildes (~) for reduplication to model complex non-concatenative phonology.

answer.text: Equals sign (=) for clitics (Rule 6), angle brackets (< >) for infixes (Rule 7), and tilde (~) for reduplication (Rule 8).

feedback.text: Correct. These dedicated operators model non-concatenative and phonologically dependent structures without confusing them with standard affixes.

answer.text: Tilde (~) for clitics, equals sign (=) for infixes, and hyphens (-) for reduplication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tilde marks reduplication and equals sign marks clitics.

answer.text: Backslash (\) for clitics, square brackets ([ ]) for infixes, and asterisks (*) for reduplication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Backslash marks non-concatenative ablaut/mutation (Rule 9) and square brackets mark inherent features (Rule 10).

answer.text: Parentheses ( ) for clitics, plus sign (+) for infixes, and colon (:) for reduplication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are not the standard operators defined in Leipzig Rules 6, 7, and 8.

name.text: 10 Question: Advanced Leipzig Operators: Non-Concatenative Morphology and Ablaut

questiontext.text: When is the backslash (\) operator used according to Leipzig Glossing Rule 9?

generalfeedback.text: Leipzig Rule 9 uses the backslash (\) to denote internal vowel gradations, Indo-European ablaut, and Semitic templatic root alternations.

answer.text: When an internal vowel gradation, Indo-European ablaut, or Semitic root-and-pattern mutation conveys grammatical meaning without concatenative affixation.

feedback.text: Correct. The backslash attaches grammatical features to lexical stems when changes occur via internal stem vowel modification (e.g., write\PST or leave\AOR).

answer.text: When separating two completely unrelated sentences in an alignment corpus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sentences are separated by standard paragraph breaks or TEI structural tags, not backslashes.

answer.text: When a word is missing from the manuscript due to a physical lacuna.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lacunae and illegible characters are encoded with TEI or , not backslashes in Rule 9.

answer.text: When an editor disagrees with a scribal reading and proposes a conjectural emendation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conjectural emendations are handled in the critical apparatus (TEI /), not via Rule 9.

name.text: 11 Question: Advanced Leipzig Operators: Zero Morphemes and Inherent Categories

questiontext.text: How do the Leipzig rules represent contrastive null morphemes and inherent non-inflected lexical categories like grammatical gender?

generalfeedback.text: Use ∅ for contrastive null morphemes and square brackets [ ] for inherent lexical categories like gender that lack dedicated affixes.

answer.text: Null morphemes are marked with ∅ or 0, while inherent lexical categories are enclosed in square brackets [ ].

feedback.text: Correct. Rule 10 uses ∅/0 for structural zeros contrasting with overt affixes, and square brackets (e.g., road[F]) for inherent lexical features.

answer.text: Null morphemes are marked with question marks (?), and inherent categories are marked with exclamation marks (!).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Non-standard punctuation introduces syntax errors into automated Leipzig parsers.

answer.text: Both null morphemes and inherent categories are omitted entirely from all annotation tiers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omitting contrastive zeros or inherent features discards vital morphological and lexical information.

answer.text: Null morphemes are enclosed in angle brackets (< >), and inherent categories are enclosed in double quotes (" ").

feedback.text: Incorrect. Angle brackets denote infixes (Rule 7), not null morphemes.

name.text: 12 Question: Pedagogical Practice: Manual 4-Line IGT of Ancient Greek

questiontext.text: In the manual 4-line IGT of the Greek verb form ποιησαίμην (from ποιέω), what is the correct morphemic segmentation on Line 2 and gloss on Line 3?

generalfeedback.text: Manual Greek IGT construction requires systematically unpacking verbal stem, aspect, mood, and person morphemes into strictly synchronized vertical tiers.

answer.text: Line 2: ποιη-σα-ί-μην | Line 3: make-AOR-OPT-1SG.MID

feedback.text: Correct. The form breaks into stem (ποιη-), aorist marker (-σα-), optative marker (-ί-), and 1st singular middle ending (-μην), with 3 hyphens matching in both tiers.

answer.text: Line 2: ποιησαίμην | Line 3: make-PST.1SG

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leaving the surface verb unsegmented fails to expose its internal aorist, optative, and middle voice morphemes.

answer.text: Line 2: ποι-η-σα-ι-μη-ν | Line 3: make-ACT-AOR-OPT-MID-1SG

feedback.text: Incorrect. Splitting every syllable arbitrarily creates phantom morphemes that do not reflect Greek morphological structure.

answer.text: Line 2: ποιη-σαίμην | Line 3: make-PASS.IND.1SG

feedback.text: Incorrect. The form is optative middle, not indicative passive, and contains separate optative and personal inflectional affixes.

name.text: 13 Question: Pedagogical Practice: Manual 4-Line IGT of a Semitic Language

questiontext.text: In Classical Syriac IGT (Peshitta John 1:1), how is the proclitic preposition in ܒ݁ܪܺܫܺܝܬ݂ ("in the beginning") properly represented on Line 2 and Line 3?

generalfeedback.text: Semitic IGT leverages clitic boundaries (=) and templatic alternations (\) to model proclitic prepositions, existential particles, and emphatic nominal states.

answer.text: Line 2: ܒ݁=ܪܺܫܺܝܬ݂ | Line 3: in=beginning.F.SG

feedback.text: Correct. Following Leipzig Rule 6, the proclitic preposition b- is joined to the host noun with an equals sign (=) in both tiers.

answer.text: Line 2: ܒ݁-ܪܺܫܺܝܬ݂ | Line 3: in-beginning.F.SG

feedback.text: Incorrect. Using a hyphen treats the syntactic clitic preposition as an inflectional prefix, violating Rule 6.

answer.text: Line 2: ܒ݁ ܪܺܫܺܝܬ݂ | Line 3: in beginning.F.SG

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inserting a space splits the single orthographic word into two tokens, violating Rule 1 token synchronization.

answer.text: Line 2: ܒ݁ܪܺܫܺܝܬ݂ | Line 3: in_the_beginning

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leaving the proclitic unsegmented fails to expose the distinct prepositional and nominal components.

name.text: 14 Question: TEI Guidelines Chapter 16: Linking, Segmentation, and Alignment

questiontext.text: What core architectural mechanism does TEI P5 Chapter 16 (§16.1) provide for parallel text alignment?

generalfeedback.text: TEI Chapter 16 (§16.1) defines and as an extensible graph network for encoding pointer-based relationships across parallel documents.

answer.text: An extensible network of and elements that declare associative relationships between XML elements via unique @xml:id pointers.

feedback.text: Correct. TEI §16.1 conceptualizes aligned documents as graph networks linked by explicit ID-based URI fragment pointers.

answer.text: A mandatory requirement that all translations be hardcoded inline inside elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI Chapter 16 promotes standoff pointer networks rather than stuffing translations into commentary notes.

answer.text: A fixed binary table that forbids linking more than two words together.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI elements support multilateral 1:N, N:1, and N:M alignments via space-delimited target pointers.

answer.text: An automated machine translation engine built directly into the TEI schema compiler.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI defines data representation standards, not automated machine translation software.

name.text: 15 Question: Sentence-Level Parallel Alignment with linkGrp and link

questiontext.text: How is sentence-level alignment encoded between parallel documents in TEI XML standoff markup?

generalfeedback.text: Sentence-level alignment assigns unique @xml:id attributes to elements and pairs them through elements in a .

answer.text: Sentences are wrapped in elements with unique @xml:id attributes and paired via within a .

feedback.text: Correct. This establishes explicit bilateral correspondences between source and target sentence nodes across document boundaries.

answer.text: Sentences are merged into a single bilingual paragraph with alternating words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Merging sentences into alternating words destroys the syntactic integrity of both texts.

answer.text: Sentences are linked by assigning them identical filenames in the file system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Filenames do not establish machine-readable XML pointer graphs between sentence elements.

answer.text: Sentences are aligned by embedding raw pixel coordinates from manuscript scans inside elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manuscript facsimile coordinates belong in IIIF or TEI / elements, not translation alignment links.

name.text: 16 Question: Tokenization and Morphological Segmentation in TEI: w and m

questiontext.text: How do TEI and elements represent fine-grained morphological segmentation in digital editions?

generalfeedback.text: TEI and elements encode word-level and morpheme-level segmentation with @lemma and @pos attributes, giving every affix a unique @xml:id.

answer.text: <w> encapsulates the grammatical word with @lemma and @pos attributes, while child <m> elements isolate individual morphemes with @type and unique @xml:id attributes.

feedback.text: Correct. This structure captures the complete word-level lexical metadata while providing stable ID targets for every individual morpheme.

answer.text: <w> is used exclusively for punctuation marks, while <m> encodes entire sentences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation is encoded with , sentences with , words with , and morphemes with .

answer.text: <w> and <m> cannot be nested and must be placed in separate XML documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. elements are standardly nested directly inside parent elements.

answer.text: <w> strips all diacritical marks from historical texts to simplify search indexes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI elements preserve full historical orthography while storing normalized forms in attributes like @lemma.

name.text: 17 Question: Standoff vs. Inline Alignment Markup in TEI

questiontext.text: Why is standoff alignment considered the scholarly gold standard over inline alignment in collaborative critical editions?

generalfeedback.text: Standoff alignment isolates alignment links in separate files via and , enabling clean multi-translation scaling and collaborative version control.

answer.text: It keeps primary source files pristine and read-only, allows multiple translations to scale independently, and prevents Git merge conflicts across distributed teams.

feedback.text: Correct. Standoff markup cleanly separates source philology, morphological analysis, and translation links into independent, modular files.

answer.text: It is the only alignment format supported by web browsers without requiring CSS or JavaScript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web browsers require transformation (XSLT/JS) for both inline and standoff XML.

answer.text: It reduces the file size of the digital edition by deleting the original manuscript transcriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standoff markup preserves all primary transcriptions in their entirety.

answer.text: Inline alignment is prohibited by the TEI P5 Guidelines under all circumstances.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inline alignment with @corresp is permitted for simple texts, but standoff is preferred for complex multi-translation editions.

name.text: 18 Question: Modeling Complex Alignments in TEI: 1-to-Many and Many-to-Many Links

questiontext.text: How does TEI Chapter 16 represent non-isomorphic alignments (1:N, N:1, N:M) and discontinuous multi-word units?

generalfeedback.text: TEI supports 1:N, N:1, and N:M alignments by listing multiple URIs, while binds discontinuous tokens into virtual units.

answer.text: <link targets="..."/> accepts multiple space-delimited URIs, while <join> elements bind discontinuous tokens into virtual compound units.

feedback.text: Correct. Listing multiple target IDs handles n-ary correspondences, and unites split idioms (such as tmesis or phrasal verbs) before linking.

answer.text: Non-isomorphic alignments are strictly forbidden; every source word must map to exactly one target word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Real translation is filled with asymmetric correspondences that TEI natively accommodates.

answer.text: Discontinuous tokens must be physically reordered in the XML source file to stand adjacent to one another.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reordering words corrupts the physical transcription of the manuscript witness.

answer.text: 1:N alignments require duplicating the source word XML element multiple times in the base text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Duplicating source elements corrupts the transcription and creates duplicate XML IDs.

name.text: 19 Question: Zero-Alignment and Ellipsis in TEI

questiontext.text: Why must zero-alignments (untranslated particles or translated ellipses) be explicitly encoded rather than omitted from alignment files?

generalfeedback.text: Zero-alignments (1:0 and 0:1) must be explicitly encoded using unary links, #NULL pointers, or elements to distinguish intentional omissions from errors.

answer.text: Explicit encoding (via unary links, #NULL targets, or ) distinguishes intentional omissions from accidental editorial oversights and ensures complete token accountability.

feedback.text: Correct. If an unaligned token is simply omitted, validation scripts and statistical evaluators cannot determine whether the omission was deliberate.

answer.text: The TEI XML parser crashes immediately if any word in the source file lacks a target translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML parsers do not crash on missing links, but data completeness and error auditing require accounting for every token.

answer.text: Zero-alignment requires deleting the untranslated word from the primary critical text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial transcriptions must never delete authentic manuscript words simply because a translator omitted them.

answer.text: Explicit zero-alignments are required to automatically generate modern English audio narration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The purpose of zero-alignment encoding is philological accountability and statistical evaluation.

name.text: 20 Question: Interlinear Glossing in TEI: The interlinear Pattern and gloss

questiontext.text: How does the TEI pattern structure four-line interlinear data within a single document?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI structure pairs morphemes directly with elements, enabling robust CSS/XSLT interlinear rendering and morphosyntactic querying.

answer.text: It nests morphemes directly alongside child elements within each , concluding with a for the sentence.

feedback.text: Correct. This hierarchical structure pairs morphemes and glosses locally, facilitating CSS/XSLT interlinear rendering and morphosyntactic queries.

answer.text: It places all morphemes in the and all glosses in an external CSV spreadsheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The IGT pattern integrates morphemes and glosses directly in the text body inside .

answer.text: It requires converting all Greek and Hebrew scripts into Latin phonetic transcriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI preserves authentic historical scripts and Unicode encodings in Line 1 and Line 2.

answer.text:
It replaces XML markup with plain ASCII column tabs inside a 

 element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. While plain text uses tabs, TEI encodes the structure using formal XML elements like , , and .

name.text: 21 Question: Morphosyntactic Feature Structures in TEI

questiontext.text: What is the primary advantage of mapping Leipzig abbreviations to TEI Feature Structures ( and ) and ISO 24610 standards?

generalfeedback.text: TEI (Feature Structures) unpacks concatenated Leipzig strings into formal, machine-readable feature-value pairs linked to international linguistic ontologies.

answer.text: It unpacks concatenated abbreviation strings into standardized, ontologically grounded feature-value pairs, eliminating terminological ambiguity across international corpora.

feedback.text: Correct. Linking morphemes to elements connects digital critical editions to international linguistic ontologies (such as ISOcat and Universal Dependencies).

answer.text: It automatically translates the critical edition into thirty modern European languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Feature structures represent linguistic metadata, not automated machine translations.

answer.text: It compresses XML file sizes by converting text into binary executable code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Feature structures are verbose, explicit XML markup designed for semantic clarity, not file compression.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for human editors to transcribe manuscript witnesses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linguistic tagging is applied to human-curated transcriptions.

name.text: 22 Question: Aligning Across Writing Systems and Orthographies

questiontext.text: What attributes must be declared on structural XML elements when aligning bidirectional texts (such as Hebrew/Syriac and Greek/English)?

generalfeedback.text: Cross-script alignment requires explicit @xml:lang and @dir declarations on all elements to prevent Unicode BiDi rendering distortions across LTR and RTL texts.

answer.text: Explicit @xml:lang tags (e.g. hbo, syc, grc, en) and @dir attributes (ltr or rtl) to prevent Unicode BiDi rendering distortions.

feedback.text: Correct. Explicit language and direction declarations ensure that rendering engines and alignment tools do not misplace punctuation or gloss numbers across RTL and LTR scripts.

answer.text: A @font attribute naming a proprietary TrueType font installed on the editor's local computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions rely on open Unicode standards and standard web fonts, not local proprietary font names.

answer.text: An @encoding attribute set to ASCII-7 to strip non-Latin characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical editions require full UTF-8 Unicode support to preserve polytonic Greek and Semitic scripts.

answer.text: A @transliteration attribute converting all Semitic letters into Latin digits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual scholarship works directly with authentic historical scripts.

name.text: 23 Question: Designing the Human Gold Standard

questiontext.text: In the design of an authoritative alignment gold standard, what is the distinction between Sure (S) and Possible (P) links?

generalfeedback.text: A gold standard requires rigorous annotation guidelines and must categorize alignments into Sure (S) and Possible (P) links for mathematical evaluation.

answer.text: Sure links (S) represent unambiguous, grammatically mandatory correspondences, while Possible links (P) include idiomatic, paraphrastic, or loose equivalents.

feedback.text: Correct. Formalized by Och and Ney (2003), the S vs. P distinction prevents automated tools from being penalized for plausible but non-mandatory translational links.

answer.text: Sure links are created by computer algorithms, while Possible links are created by human students.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both Sure and Possible links are established by human expert annotators when authoring gold standards.

answer.text: Sure links apply only to nouns, while Possible links apply to verbs and adjectives.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The distinction reflects translational certainty and literalness, not grammatical part of speech.

answer.text: Sure links are published in the edition, while Possible links are discarded permanently before release.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both link sets are preserved in the gold standard dataset for mathematical evaluation.

name.text: 24 Question: Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA) in Manual Alignment

questiontext.text: What do empirical studies in digital classics (such as the Ugarit benchmarks) reveal about Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA) between expert philologists?

generalfeedback.text: Inter-annotator agreement measures human consistency (κ and F1); empirical benchmarks show expert philologists achieve ~86–91% agreement on historical bitexts.

answer.text: Trained philologists achieve ~86% to 91.5% word-level alignment agreement, with disagreements centering primarily on untranslated particles, idioms, and ellipsis resolution.

feedback.text: Correct. Disagreements stem from differing editorial philosophies regarding functional particles and loose idioms rather than grammatical ignorance.

answer.text: Philologists achieve 100% identical alignments across all texts regardless of genre.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Natural language ambiguity and translational divergence inevitably produce ~10% variation between independent annotators.

answer.text: Agreement between human scholars is typically below 30%, proving that translation alignment is entirely subjective.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High IAA (~86–91%) demonstrates that alignment is a rigorous, highly consistent scientific discipline when guided by clear standards.

answer.text: Inter-annotator agreement can only be measured on modern technical manuals and cannot be applied to ancient languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. IAA is standard practice in historical corpus linguistics and digital philology.

name.text: 25 Question: Resolving Philological Disagreements in Glossing

questiontext.text: How does TEI XML represent polysemy, double entendre, or competing scholarly interpretations within an alignment graph?

generalfeedback.text: TEI elements support multiple competing alignments with @resp and attributes, transparently preserving polysemy and scholarly debate.

answer.text: By authoring multiple competing elements pointing to the same source word, differentiated by @resp attributes and explanatory children.

feedback.text: Correct. TEI standoff alignment does not force an artificial consensus; it transparently preserves alternative interpretive readings with full attribution.

answer.text: By randomly deleting all but one reading during XML compilation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions aim to preserve and document scholarly divergence, not suppress it.

answer.text: By converting the XML document into a flat plain-text file without markup.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Plain text cannot represent multi-layered attributed graphs.

answer.text: By requiring the lead editor to permanently ban any alternative interpretations from the repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly integrity requires transparently documenting polysemy and competing interpretations.

name.text: 26 Question: Step-by-Step Manual Workflow: From Source Transcription to TEI IGT

questiontext.text: What is the final technical verification step in the six-stage manual alignment workflow before committing to Git?

generalfeedback.text: The six-stage manual workflow enforces rigorous progression from tokenization through Leipzig glossing to schema-validated TEI standoff markup.

name.text: 27 Question: Tooling Support for Manual Alignment: Text Editors and XML Schema Validation

questiontext.text: Which tool and command provides the fastest automated verification of TEI XML validity against the official RelaxNG schema?

generalfeedback.text: Use monospace editors for plain-text IGT and validate TEI XML with xmllint and Python pointer verification scripts to catch syntax and reference errors.

answer.text: xmllint --noout --relaxng https://www.tei-c.org/release/xml/tei/custom/schema/relaxng/tei_all.rng

feedback.text: Correct. xmllint rapidly parses the document against the official RelaxNG schema, reporting exact line numbers for any syntax or structural defects.

answer.text: git commit --amend --no-edit

feedback.text: Incorrect. That amends the previous Git commit; it performs no XML schema validation.

answer.text: grep -r "" /home/user/

feedback.text: Incorrect. grep searches for text patterns; it cannot validate XML tree hierarchies or schema constraints.

answer.text: python3 -m http.server 8000

feedback.text: Incorrect. That launches a local web server, not an XML schema validator.
